summary: Non-habit-forming sleep-onset medication that works on melatonin receptors (MT1/MT2). Helps you fall asleep within ~30 minutes without the classic benzo/Z-drug dependence profile.
description: Rozerem is a prescription sleep medication for trouble falling asleep. It works by targeting melatonin receptors that help regulate your sleep-wake clock, rather than sedating your brain like benzodiazepines or Z-drugs. Most people take 8 mg within 30 minutes of bedtime. Avoid taking it with a high-fat meal (it slows and blunts the effect). Call your prescriber right away if you have swelling of the face/lips/tongue (angioedema) or if you have any unusual sleep behaviors.
patient_summary: Rozerem helps with sleep-onset insomnia (trouble falling asleep) by acting on melatonin receptors instead of “knocking you out.” Most people take 8 mg near bedtime. Don’t take it with a high-fat meal, and don’t mix it with fluvoxamine. If you ever have swelling (angioedema) or complex sleep behaviors, stop it and get medical help.

primary.context: FDA-labeled for insomnia characterized by difficulty falling asleep (sleep-onset insomnia).

off_label.context: Sometimes used in ICU-related delirium prevention/sleep protocols as an alternative to melatonin, when a clinician wants a melatonin-receptor option without typical sedative-hypnotic dependence risk.

If your mood dips, motivation drops, or suicidal thoughts show up, treat that as urgent and loop in your clinician.

serious_risks.risk: Hypersensitivity reactions (rare): anaphylaxis, angioedema—do not rechallenge if it occurs
Complex sleep behaviors (reported): sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls while asleep; may include amnesia—discontinue if this happens
Clinically meaningful mood worsening or suicidal ideation (reported with hypnotics)—requires urgent clinical reassessment

contraindications.contraindication: History of angioedema with previous ramelteon therapy (do not rechallenge)

precautions: Complex sleep behaviors have been reported (sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls) and may occur with amnesia; discontinue if this happens
May cause CNS depression (impaired alertness); use caution with driving or hazardous tasks—especially early on
Abnormal thinking/behavior changes have been reported with hypnotics (agitation, hallucinations, depersonalization, decreased inhibition)
Use caution in depression; worsening depression and suicidal ideation have been reported with hypnotics
Use caution in respiratory compromise (COPD, sleep apnea); not recommended in severe sleep apnea (not studied)
Hepatic impairment increases exposure substantially; not recommended in severe hepatic impairment
May affect reproductive hormones (prolactin increase, testosterone decrease); monitor if symptoms suggest hormonal disruption

interactions.mechanism: Contraindicated. Can significantly increase ramelteon exposure and side effects.
interactions.action: Do not use together. Choose a different sleep strategy if you’re on fluvoxamine.

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (alcohol, sedatives, sleep meds, some antihistamines, cannabis)
interactions.mechanism: Additive impairment and next-day sedation; may increase risk of unusual sleep behaviors.
interactions.action: Avoid alcohol. Use extra caution combining with anything sedating. If you’re already on a sedating medication, your prescriber should know.

interactions.mechanism: Can raise ramelteon levels and increase side effects like dizziness/somnolence.
interactions.action: Clinician should review your medication list for interaction risk and either avoid the combo or monitor closely.

interactions.mechanism: May reduce effectiveness by lowering medication levels.
interactions.action: If Rozerem suddenly stops working, review recent medication/supplement changes with your clinician.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Sleep target clarity: Is the problem sleep onset vs sleep maintenance vs early-morning awakening? Rozerem is mainly for sleep onset.
Next-day impairment: dizziness, sleepiness, slowed reaction time—especially early in treatment and in older adults.
Mood symptoms: worsening depression, irritability, suicidal ideation—monitor closely in anyone with depression history.
Complex sleep behaviors: sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls while asleep; discontinue if reported.
Hypersensitivity: swelling of face/lips/tongue, hives, breathing difficulty—urgent evaluation; do not rechallenge after angioedema.
Hormonal symptoms: decreased libido, menstrual disruption, galactorrhea, sexual dysfunction—consider checking prolactin and testosterone if clinically indicated.
Medication interaction review: especially CYP1A2 inhibitors/fluvoxamine and other sedatives.
If insomnia persists beyond 7 to 10 days, reassess for psychiatric/medical causes (anxiety, depression, substance use, medication effects, sleep apnea, circadian rhythm disruption).

special_populations.pregnancy: Animal reproduction studies observed adverse events. If you’re pregnant or trying to conceive, discuss non-medication insomnia treatments first (like CBT-I) and weigh risks vs benefits with your clinician.
special_populations.lactation: Ramelteon and its active metabolite (M-II) are present in breast milk. A case report estimated a low relative infant dose (RID ~0.24%). Manufacturer recommends weighing benefits vs infant exposure. If used while breastfeeding, monitor the infant for somnolence and feeding problems. Some clinicians may recommend pumping and discarding breast milk during treatment and for 25 hours after the last dose to reduce exposure.
special_populations.geriatric: Refer to adult dosing; use with caution. Older adults have higher exposure (AUC and Cmax substantially increased vs younger adults), which can increase dizziness/somnolence risk—start with strict bedtime-only use and reassess frequently.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Mild impairment: no manufacturer-provided adjustment; moderate impairment: use with caution (exposure can increase markedly). Severe impairment: use is not recommended.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Rapid; high-fat meal delays absorption and changes exposure
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Ramelteon: 1 to 2.6 hours; active metabolite (M-II): 2 to 5 hours
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive first-pass oxidative metabolism primarily via CYP1A2, with contributions from CYP2C and CYP3A4; forms active metabolite (M-II)
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Primarily as metabolites: urine (~84%) and feces (~4%)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: High-fat meal delays Tmax, reduces Cmax, and increases AUC (~31%); avoid taking with or right after a high-fat meal

dosing.titration: Ramelteon is typically taken as a single bedtime dose. It works best when it’s paired with a consistent sleep schedule and when you avoid taking it with a high-fat meal.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Rozerem is not a benzodiazepine and is not a controlled substance. In most cases, it does not require a taper and can be stopped without a withdrawal-style discontinuation plan. That said, if you stop it and your sleep rebounds worse, that’s usually your underlying insomnia returning—not a dangerous withdrawal. The fix is reassessing the sleep plan (schedule, CBT-I, anxiety management, timing of caffeine/light) rather than chasing higher and higher doses.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Rozerem is a sleep-onset medication—meaning it’s for trouble falling asleep, not a general sedative. It’s often a good fit when you want something that targets the sleep-wake system (melatonin receptors) without the same dependence profile as benzodiazepines or Z-drugs.
off_label: ICU-related sleep support and delirium prevention protocols (clinician-directed)

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Rozerem typically starts working in about 30 minutes, which is why it’s taken right before bed. It’s meant to help you fall asleep—not to keep you asleep all night.
key_points: Short parent half-life (1 to 2.6 hours), with an active metabolite lasting longer (2 to 5 hours)
High-fat meals can delay and blunt the bedtime effect—avoid taking it with or right after a heavy, fatty dinner

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Rozerem’s sweet spot is sleep onset: it helps some people fall asleep faster and reduces that “stuck awake” feeling at bedtime. It’s not usually the best standalone choice if your main problem is waking up repeatedly or waking up too early—those patterns often need different strategies (behavioral work, addressing anxiety, or a medication that targets sleep maintenance).
sections.clinical_details: Clinically, Rozerem is often chosen when a prescriber wants a non-controlled, melatonin-receptor approach—especially for people with a history of substance use, sensitivity to sedatives, or concern about dependence. Response is very individual, and bedtime habits matter a lot (light exposure, caffeine timing, screens, and consistent wake time).

sections.intro: Ramelteon is heavily affected by metabolism interactions (especially CYP1A2). Some combinations can drastically raise levels and side effects.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Rozerem is not a benzodiazepine and is not a controlled substance. In most cases, it does not require a taper and can be stopped without a withdrawal-style discontinuation plan. That said, if you stop it and your sleep rebounds worse, that’s usually your underlying insomnia returning—not a dangerous withdrawal. The fix is reassessing the sleep plan (schedule, CBT-I, anxiety management, timing of caffeine/light) rather than chasing higher and higher doses.
key_points: Taper is usually not necessary for ramelteon
If sleep gets worse after stopping, think “return of insomnia,” not “medical withdrawal emergency”
If you were relying on it nightly, consider transitioning to CBT-I habits so sleep isn’t dependent on a pill
If mood symptoms worsen during start/stop, treat that as clinically important and follow up

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Ramelteon is typically taken as a single bedtime dose. It works best when it’s paired with a consistent sleep schedule and when you avoid taking it with a high-fat meal.

adult.sleep_onset_prn_use: 8 mg PO once daily within 30 minutes of bedtime, as needed. Maximum dose: 8 mg/day.
adult.icu_delirium_prevention_bedtime: 8 mg PO once daily at bedtime (off-label; clinician-directed ICU protocols).

sections.simple_explanation: This is a melatonin-receptor sleep-onset medication. You take one dose near bedtime. More is not better—8 mg is the max, and taking it with a heavy fatty meal can delay the effect.

sections.text: Use extra caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, and liver disease. Ramelteon exposure increases significantly with hepatic impairment and is not recommended in severe liver impairment.

Some clinicians may recommend pumping and discarding breast milk during treatment and for 25 hours after the last dose to reduce exposure.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Ramelteon is available as an 8 mg tablet (brand and generic). Tablets are typically swallowed whole. High-fat meals can interfere with timing and effect, so bedtime dosing works best when it’s not paired with a heavy fatty dinner.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Rozerem is a potent, selective agonist at melatonin receptors MT1 and MT2 in the brain’s circadian control center (the suprachiasmatic nucleus). MT1 activation is thought to promote sleepiness, while MT2 activation helps regulate circadian timing. Unlike sedatives that broadly slow brain activity, this medication is more like a targeted “sleep signal” aimed at sleep initiation.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Rozerem fits best for sleep-onset insomnia—especially when you want to avoid controlled substances, dependence risk, and heavy sedation. It’s often paired with CBT-I and sleep routine changes (consistent wake time, light management, caffeine timing). In higher-risk patients (substance use history, sensitivity to sedatives, older adults), it can be an appealing first medication trial. If insomnia is driven by anxiety, trauma, depression, or a circadian rhythm mismatch, treating the underlying driver usually matters more than any single sleep pill.

faqs.a: Rozerem (ramelteon) is used for sleep-onset insomnia—trouble falling asleep. It’s not primarily for staying asleep all night, and it’s not meant to work like a heavy sedative.

faqs.q: How do I take ramelteon correctly?
faqs.a: Take 8 mg within 30 minutes of bedtime, only when you can actually go to bed. After you take it, keep your activities limited to getting ready for sleep. Don’t take it with or right after a high-fat meal.
Onset is about 30 minutes for many people. That’s why it’s dosed right before bed instead of earlier in the evening.

faqs.q: Can I take Rozerem every night?
faqs.a: Some people do, but long-term use should be intentional. If insomnia lasts beyond a couple of weeks, the goal is to treat the cause (stress, anxiety, depression, substances, schedule, sleep apnea) and use CBT-I strategies—not just keep stacking meds.

faqs.q: Is Rozerem addictive or a controlled substance?
faqs.a: It’s not a controlled substance and it’s not a benzodiazepine or a Z-drug. It works on melatonin receptors. That said, any sleep medication can become a psychological crutch if the underlying insomnia drivers aren’t addressed.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest drug interaction to know?
faqs.a: Fluvoxamine. The combination is contraindicated because it can significantly raise ramelteon levels and side effects. Always tell your prescriber about all meds and supplements.

faqs.q: Can Rozerem cause weird sleep behaviors like sleepwalking or sleep-driving?
faqs.a: Complex sleep behaviors have been reported (sleep-driving, cooking/eating, phone calls while asleep), sometimes with amnesia. If anything like that happens, stop the medication and contact your clinician immediately.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Dizziness, sleepiness (somnolence), and fatigue are the most common. Nausea and mood changes (including depression) can also happen.

faqs.q: Is Rozerem safe if I have depression or anxiety?
faqs.a: It can be used, but it requires attention. Hypnotics have been associated with mood worsening and suicidal ideation in some people. If your mood dips after starting it, don’t ignore that—tell your prescriber.

faqs.q: What if my sleep doesn’t improve after a week?
faqs.a: If insomnia doesn’t improve after 7 to 10 days, that’s a prompt to reassess the cause. Sleep problems often come from anxiety, depression, substances, medication side effects, sleep apnea, circadian rhythm issues, or inconsistent schedules—fixing the driver matters more than swapping pills.

faqs.q: Can I take ramelteon if I have liver or kidney problems?
faqs.a: Kidney impairment typically doesn’t require a dose adjustment. Liver impairment is different: exposure can increase a lot, and it’s not recommended in severe hepatic impairment. Your prescriber should factor this in.

faqs.q: Can I take Rozerem while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Ramelteon and its metabolite are present in breast milk. A case report estimated low infant exposure, but the decision should weigh infant exposure risk vs benefits to the parent. If used, monitor the baby for sleepiness and feeding problems; some clinicians may recommend pumping and discarding milk during treatment and for 25 hours after the last dose.
